strengths: Identifies and formalizes a practically relevant but underexplored problem: multi-period 3D reconstruction with long-term, discontinuous geometry and appearance changes, distinct from static and smooth-dynamic settings.
Introduces the ChronoScene benchmark with real and synthetic multi-period scenes (8,891 images, 12 scenes, 42 sub-scenes), released publicly with code, which is likely useful for future research.

The proposed ChronoGS is clearly described and reasonably designed: an anchor scaffold of union geometry with invariant base features, local/global period-varying features, temporal encoding, and a geometry activation mechanism.

Experiments report consistent improvements over adapted static and dynamic baselines on both real and synthetic scenes, with lower memory and training iterations than per-period independent training; ablations support the role of each feature component.
The paper is well written and well organized, with informative figures and supplementary details on implementation, dataset statistics, and additional qualitative results.
weaknesses: The main quantitative comparison is not fully convincing: static baselines in Table 1 are trained jointly across periods, which is a weak baseline. The authors' own Table 2 shows per-period independent 3DGS/Scaffold-GS can be much stronger (e.g., 22.23 vs 18.79 PSNR on Overstreet), yet this fairer baseline is evaluated only on one scene. The claim that per-period training does not improve results contradicts Table 2.

No empirical comparison is provided to prior long-term/change-aware reconstruction methods such as Neural Scene Chronology, GaussianUpdate, or geometry-changing in-the-wild methods, despite claiming to be the first to address multi-period reconstruction.

The central claim of disentangling invariants and changes is not quantitatively evaluated: there are no metrics for temporal consistency, change localization/separation, or intermediate-state synthesis, only qualitative visualizations.

Method novelty is incremental over Scaffold-GS: the temporal model largely adds time-indexed per-period feature embeddings and opacity-based activation to an anchor-based Gaussian framework, with limited architectural innovation.

Real-scene dataset construction relies on GPS priors and manual human-in-the-loop alignment; the accuracy and robustness of cross-period registration are not quantified, which matters for the union-geometry scaffold.

Synthetic scenes are manually edited from Matrix City, potentially limiting diversity, and the evaluation protocol only assesses within-period held-out views rather than cross-period novel view synthesis.

strengths: Addresses a novel and practically important problem: multi-period 3D reconstruction where geometry and appearance change discontinuously across long time gaps, which existing static and dynamic Gaussian pipelines are not designed to handle.

Introduces ChronoScene, a new benchmark with 8,891 images across 12 real/synthetic scenes and 42 sub-scenes, aligned in a common coordinate frame with per-period point clouds; this is a useful community resource and supports reproducibility (code/data stated public).

The proposed ChronoGS is technically sound and well motivated: a unified anchor scaffold with invariant base features, local/global period-varying features, temporal encoding, explicit Gaussian offsets, and an opacity-based geometry activation mechanism to model stable vs. changing structure.

Experiments show consistent quantitative gains across real and synthetic scenes on PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS (Table 1), while Table 2 demonstrates efficiency benefits over per-period independent static training (e.g., 0.57GB vs 4.9GB and 40k vs 120k iterations on Overstreet).

Ablations in Table 3 and Fig. 8 validate the contribution of the base, local period-varying, and global period-varying features; qualitative comparisons (Figs. 6, 7, 9, 10) show sharper period-specific details and less ghosting/smearing than baselines.
The paper is generally clear and includes supplementary implementation details, dataset statistics, and additional qualitative results.
weaknesses: The core claim of disentangling/reconstructing geometry is not supported by any quantitative geometry metric. Evaluation is image-based only (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS); the dataset includes sparse point clouds, so depth/Chamfer/point-cloud metrics or cross-period geometric consistency could have been reported.

A highly relevant continual/changing-environment baseline, GaussianUpdate [29], is cited but not compared, and Neural Scene Chronology [12] is also not evaluated; the empirical case would be stronger with at least a discussion or comparison.

Baseline fairness is only partially addressed. In Table 1 the static baselines are trained jointly on mixed multi-period data, which is a known failure mode; per-period independent training is shown only for Overstreet (Table 2), not across all scenes.

Temporal interpolation is demonstrated qualitatively (Fig. 7) but not quantitatively. There is no ground-truth intermediate data, but metrics on held-out intermediate captures or temporal consistency measures would substantiate the claim of synthesizing plausible intermediate states.

Some methodological details and notation need clarification: in Eq. (2), the ⊙ operation between g(t) ∈ R^{T×d_g} / f_i^{var}(t) ∈ R^{T×d_v} and e(t) ∈ R^T is not dimensionally defined; the covariance MLP with 'no final activation' does not explain how positive scales/covariances are ensured; these details hinder reproducibility.

The geometry activation mechanism (opacity < 0) is central but not quantitatively ablated in the main paper, and its behavior for topology changes (new construction, removed structures) is not isolated from other components.
The dataset, while valuable, is limited to urban aerial/street scenes with only six real scenes; broader real-world multi-period diversity and a limitations discussion are absent.

strengths: Formalizes a practically relevant and genuinely underexplored setting—multi-period reconstruction with discontinuous geometry and appearance changes—clearly distinguishing it from static and smooth-dynamic assumptions.
Introduces ChronoScene, a non-trivial benchmark (8,891 images, 12 scenes, real + synthetic) registered into a common world frame, which could catalyze future work on long-term scene understanding.

The method is a sensible, well-motivated extension of anchor-based 3DGS: disentangling a time-invariant base feature, a local period-varying feature pool, and a global period-varying feature, with one-hot/interpolated temporal encoding.
Practical efficiency: joint multi-period optimization attains comparable or better quality than per-period training at substantially lower storage (0.57GB vs 4.9GB for per-period 3DGS in Table 2).
Reasonably thorough ablations of the three feature components and their dimensions, plus clear figures and generally readable exposition.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core is Scaffold-GS augmented with a one-hot time code modulating additive features, a standard conditioning scheme. The 'temporal encoding' and interpolation are conventional, and the claimed 'geometry activation' (negative decoded opacity) is a minor trick.

Problematic evaluation design: static/in-the-wild baselines (3DGS, Scaffold-GS, GS-W) are effectively strawmen for a task that explicitly requires per-period geometry and appearance changes, which inflates the apparent gains in Table 1. The only fair comparison (per-period independent training, Table 2) shows a modest ~0.4 dB PSNR gain over per-period 3DGS, and this comparison is restricted to a single scene (Overstreet).

Missing comparisons to the most directly relevant prior work on long-term/change modeling: NeuSC and GaussianUpdate are cited and discussed in Related Work but are never evaluated, even though they target exactly the changing-environment setting.

Numerical inconsistencies that undermine confidence in the main results: Table 1's 'Avg' columns do not match the per-scene values (e.g., Ours real-scene average is reported as 22.16 while the listed per-scene PSNRs average to ~23.3; Scaffold-GS 16.37 vs ~17.5), and Overstreet PSNR for Ours is 22.46 in Table 1 but 22.66 in Table 2 despite the stated 'same evaluation setting.'

The claim of synthesizing 'plausible intermediate states' rests on linear interpolation between one-hot period codes, which is essentially a feature blend; the evidence (Fig. 7) is purely qualitative and does not establish physically meaningful transitions.

Dataset composition limits generality: synthetic scenes are produced by manual asset edits on MatrixCity, and the six 'real' scenes are all aerial/drone captures with hard-to-verify geometric changes; temporal gaps and scene diversity are narrow.

The central geometry-activation mechanism is not ablated, and the 'first work to formally address multi-period reconstruction' claim is fuzzy given existing long-term change methods (NeuSC, GaussianUpdate) that model appearance change over time.

strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored and practically relevant problem: reconstructing multi-period scenes where both geometry and appearance change discontinuously over long time gaps.

The proposed ChronoGS framework is technically reasonable, combining anchor-based Scaffold-GS representation with period-invariant base features, per-anchor local period-varying features, a global period-varying feature, temporal encoding with interpolation, and an opacity-based geometry activation mechanism.

The introduction of the ChronoScene benchmark is a valuable contribution: it provides 8,891 images across 12 scenes and 42 sub-scenes, with real and synthetic multi-period captures aligned in a common coordinate frame.

Experiments are extensive, comparing against seven representative baselines on ChronoScene, including static, dynamic, in-the-wild, and incremental methods, with additional results on WAT, CL-Splats, and NeuSC datasets.

Ablations validate the roles of the base feature, local period-varying feature, and global period-varying feature, and show that joint multi-period optimization improves quality while reducing training iterations and memory compared with per-period independent training.
The method achieves strong quantitative results, especially on synthetic scenes, and qualitative figures demonstrate sharper period-specific geometry and appearance than baselines.
Temporal interpolation between observed periods is demonstrated qualitatively, showing the model can synthesize plausible intermediate states rather than simply blending neighboring periods.
The paper is generally clear, well-organized, and includes supplementary implementation details, extra ablations, and dataset statistics to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim of disentangling invariant structure from changes is not directly evaluated: the main metrics are within-period held-out view rendering scores, which do not measure cross-period consistency, correctness of the shared geometry, or explicit separation of invariant versus changing components.

Temporal interpolation is only shown qualitatively; no quantitative evaluation of intermediate-period synthesis or change detection is provided, even though the synthetic data could potentially support such ground truth.

Methodological novelty is moderate: the approach largely extends Scaffold-GS with per-period feature modulation, temporal one-hot/interpolated encoding, and an opacity-threshold activation, which resembles existing ideas in dynamic/4D Gaussian splatting and incremental neural rendering.

The main quantitative table lacks per-period static baselines; only Table 2 on Overstreet compares per-period independent training, where static baselines are stronger than their jointly trained counterparts in the main table, making the main comparison less informative.

The geometry activation mechanism thresholds decoded opacity below zero, where opacity is produced by a tanh activation; this is non-standard for alpha compositing, creates a hard non-differentiable exclusion, and is not ablated or analyzed for stability.

Dataset scale and diversity are limited: 12 scenes, mostly urban, and the synthetic scenes are manually edited from Matrix City; real-scene alignment relies on GPS priors and human-in-the-loop refinement without quantifying registration accuracy or its impact on evaluation.
The paper does not include a limitations section and does not discuss failure cases, such as severe structural changes that may not be captured by fixed anchor offsets and opacity gating.

The "first" claim is somewhat overstated: prior work on multi-period scene chronology and long-term scene evolution exists, even if ChronoGS is the first to cast this setting in a unified differentiable Gaussian-splatting framework.

Reproducibility is partially promised but not fully verifiable from the manuscript: the code/dataset URL is not visible in the submitted pages, and key dataset construction details are deferred to the supplementary material.

strengths: Targets an important and underexplored problem: reconstructing multi-period scenes with discrete, long-term geometry and appearance changes, where static and smooth-dynamic assumptions fail.

Proposes ChronoGS, a clean anchor-based Gaussian-splatting framework that decomposes each anchor into invariant base features, local period-varying features, and a global period-varying feature, with temporal encoding and opacity-based geometry activation.

Introduces ChronoScene, a substantial benchmark (8,891 images, 12 scenes, 42 sub-scenes, real and synthetic) aligned across periods, which is a valuable contribution to long-term 3D scene understanding.

Reports strong quantitative gains over representative static and dynamic baselines on ChronoScene and additional benchmarks (WAT, CL-Splats), with lower memory and training iterations than per-period independent training.
Ablations verify the roles of base, local period-varying, and global period-varying features; qualitative results show sharper period-specific reconstruction than baselines.
Method is clearly described overall, with supplementary implementation details, hyperparameters, and training strategy; code/dataset are promised to be public.
The temporal geometry activation and fixed Gaussian offsets are simple, effective design choices for handling discontinuous changes while maintaining cross-period consistency.
weaknesses: The method assumes known period identifiers and pre-aligned captures; it does not address inference of temporal ordering or registration errors in the wild, limiting applicability to unlabeled multi-period collections.

The paper claims to 'disentangle' invariants and changes, but evaluation is primarily rendering metrics; no direct quantitative evaluation of invariant/change separation (e.g., geometry accuracy per period, change segmentation) is provided.
Temporal interpolation is only qualitatively evaluated (Fig. 7); no quantitative metric for plausible intermediate states or cross-period view synthesis is reported.

The primary benchmark is new and self-created; although additional benchmarks are included, some baseline comparisons on ChronoScene may be unfavorable because static/dynamic methods are not designed for discrete multi-period data. On NeuSC, ChronoGS underperforms the specialized NeuSC method.

Ablations are limited: main component ablation covers only two real scenes, and feature-dimension/initialization ablations each use a single scene, with no error bars or statistical significance testing.

Several method details are ambiguous in the main paper: how g(t) and f_i^var(t) are retrieved/interpolated for continuous t, dimension matching in Eq. 2, and the photometric loss weight lambda. The supplement helps but main text could be clearer.

The geometry activation mechanism (opacity < 0) is heuristic; no ablation isolates its effect, and it is unclear whether excluded Gaussians can be reliably reactivated across periods without anchor growth.

Dataset construction relies on COLMAP/GPS and human-in-the-loop alignment; reproducibility and geographic/domain diversity are not fully characterized. Memory scaling with the number of periods is not thoroughly analyzed.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and practically relevant problem: multi-period scene reconstruction where geometry and appearance change discontinuously over long time gaps (months to years), which static 3DGS/NeRF and smooth-motion dynamic methods are not designed to handle. The motivation (city re-scanning, construction monitoring, disaster assessment) is concrete and well articulated.

Introduces ChronoScene, a non-trivial benchmark contribution: 8,891 images across 12 scenes and 42 period instances, combining real aerial/street captures with 1-3 year gaps and synthetic scenes from MatrixCity with controlled, manually edited changes; it includes calibrated poses, per-image period IDs, common world coordinates, and useful statistics (Tab. 8, Figs. 11-22). This fills a genuine gap in long-term 3D reconstruction evaluation.

The method is technically sound and well engineered on top of an anchor-based scaffold: a period-invariant base feature, per-anchor local period-varying features, and a global period-varying feature are combined via a temporal encoding (Eq. 1-2), decoded into Gaussian attributes by a lightweight MLP, with explicit per-anchor Gaussian offsets for geometric stability, opacity-based geometry activation, and anchor growth/pruning. Ablations (Tab. 3) confirm each component contributes.

Results are consistent and broad: ChronoGS achieves the best PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on both real and synthetic splits of ChronoScene (Tab. 1) with a compact memory footprint, and is also competitive on the WAT and CL-Splats benchmarks (Tabs. 9-10).

A genuine efficiency argument is provided in Tab. 2: joint multi-period optimization attains comparable or better quality with 40k iterations and 0.57 GB versus 120k iterations and ~4.9 GB for per-period static training, reducing storage and compute substantially.

Reproducibility is good: implementation details (feature dims, MLP architecture, learning rates, training phases, grid size, thresholds) are reported, and code plus the dataset are promised for release.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is incremental. The framework is essentially Scaffold-GS augmented with period-conditioned features/embeddings; the 'disentanglement' is a standard invariant-vs-varying latent decomposition, and the geometry activation is an opacity gating heuristic closely related to Scaffold-GS opacity-based pruning. The claim of being 'the first work to reconstruct multi-period scenes within a unified, differentiable Gaussian-splatting framework' is overstated given existing long-term/continual 3DGS works (CL-Splats, GaussianUpdate, GsEditor) that also model evolving scenes, and the distinction from 'incremental' methods is argued rather than demonstrated.

The headline comparison (Tab. 1) is not a fair test of the claimed advantage: static baselines (3DGS, Scaffold-GS, GS-W) are trained jointly across all periods, which forces temporal averaging and is expected to fail under inconsistent geometry. The fairer per-period training comparison (Tab. 2) shows only a marginal PSNR gain (22.66 vs 22.23 on Overstreet), so the dramatic gaps in the main table largely reflect a mismatched baseline rather than a decisive modeling advance.

The most relevant baselines are missing from the proposed benchmark. CL-Splats, GaussianUpdate, and GsEditor, which specifically target long-term/continual scene evolution, are not evaluated on ChronoScene in the main paper; they appear only on other benchmarks in the supplementary (Tabs. 9-11), where ChronoGS is actually worse than NeuSC on NeuSC. This leaves unresolved whether ChronoGS truly handles discontinuous changes better than methods designed for that setting.

The temporal interpolation claim is unsupported. Eq. (1) linearly interpolates one-hot period embeddings and Fig. 7 shows renders at intermediate t, but no intermediate ground truth exists, so 'plausible intermediate states' is asserted rather than measured. Moreover, because period features are learned per observed period, the model cannot generalize to a genuinely unseen period, which limits its practical value and is not discussed.

Dataset construction is under-specified and potentially biased. Real scenes rely on GPS priors plus human-in-the-loop refinement to a common frame, and synthetic scenes are manually edited; the paper does not quantify the magnitude of change per period, verify alignment quality, or analyze how these choices affect the benchmark and the reported metrics.

The evaluation only measures within-period novel-view synthesis and never directly evaluates the central 'disentangling invariants and changes' claim (e.g., change localization/separation quality, or extrapolation to a held-out period). Ablation margins are also small on some scenes (e.g., Lawncourt full 22.16 vs w/o Global 22.11 in Tab. 3), weakening the strength of the component analysis.

Minor issues: the abstract ends with 'publicly available at' without a URL; the definition of '42 sub-scenes' (periods) is confusing and inconsistent with the 12 scenes in Tab. 8; the opacity<0 activation threshold and its interaction with alpha compositing and gradient flow lack a sensitivity analysis.
